title: CAT: Interpretable Concept-based Taylor Additive Models

problem.claim: Feature-based Generalized Additive Models require many parameters, are prone to overfitting, are difficult to train and scale, and become less interpretable when datasets contain many features.

gap.claim: Concept-based interpretable methods require extensive domain-expert annotation of concept names and ground-truth values.

contributions.claim: CAT is an interpretable concept-based Taylor additive model that removes the need for domain experts to annotate concepts and their ground-truth values.

CAT groups input features, embeds each group into a one-dimensional high-level concept representation, and feeds those representations into a white-box TaylorNet that models input-output relationships with polynomials.
CAT explains model predictions through high-level concepts.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors describe CAT as a novel interpretable concept-based Taylor additive model.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Across multiple benchmarks, CAT reportedly outperforms or competes with baselines while using fewer model parameters.
CAT reportedly explains model predictions effectively through high-level concepts.

narrative_sequence.summary: Generalized Additive Models learn feature-wise nonlinear functions and combine them for prediction.
Feature-based GAMs have scaling, overfitting, training, and human-interpretability limitations.
Concept-based methods improve explanation framing but depend on extensive expert concept annotation.
CAT uses user-provided feature groups, learned one-dimensional concept representations, and a polynomial TaylorNet.
The authors report competitive benchmark performance, reduced parameter needs, and high-level concept explanations.

source_observation.claim: Grouping input features into broad categories can support concept-based explanations without requiring expert labels for concept names and ground-truth values.

interpretation.claim: Lightweight metadata-based structure may reduce annotation burden while retaining a human-oriented explanatory layer.

application.claim: When designing interpretable models, consider user-supplied feature grouping as an alternative to fully labeled intermediate concepts.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish how well this approach works when feature groups are ambiguous, poorly chosen, or domain-specific.

unknowns: The abstract does not identify the benchmarks, datasets, metrics, or comparison conditions.
The abstract does not quantify parameter reductions or performance differences.
The abstract does not describe the TaylorNet architecture, training procedure, or polynomial degree.
The abstract does not establish the quality of the concept explanations through human evaluation or other independent verification.
